# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This thesis studied how the content of the context window shapes the fraud-detection performance of tabular foundation models (TFMs) under extreme class imbalance. Five TFMs and two GBDT baselines trained on the full data were evaluated on five public fraud datasets with fraud rates between 0.13 % and 1.5 %. With TFMs the model weights stayed frozen, and all adaptation happened through in-context learning. Four experimental conditions spanned the design space described in @sec-methods: a random context (C1), a stratified context with an enforced fraud ratio (C2), a kNN-retrieved context at the natural ratio (C3) and the full RAP combination of retrieval and ratio control (C4).

Each research question described in @sec-intro-rqs received a unambiguous  answer. On research question 1, zero-shot TFMs restricted to a 50,000-row random context were competitive with untuned GBDTs trained on the full training data, with two wins, one tie and two losses across the five datasets elaborated further in @sec-results-rq1. On second research question, stratified balancing lifted every model on every dataset, and the gain was largest where the context window was smallest. The optimal ratio is a broad plateau ranging roughly from 5 to 10 % fraud and it starts to hurt only once fraud-row duplication kicks in. The practical rule is to include enough fraud, roughly 10 % when that requires no heavy duplication. Further results are accounted in @sec-results-rq2.

The relevance lever was an unambiguous failure. On third research quetsion, kNN retrieval at the natural ratio never beat the random context and was catastrophic where retrieval collapsed. An ablation study attributes the damage to the retrieved non-fraudulent rows, which strip the negative class of its diversity. On eu_cc dataset the performance degraded through fraud depletion and duplication. On fourth research question, combining retrieval with ratio control stayed below plain stratified balancing on every dataset. The performance for full RAP pipeline could not be helped with finetuning as it is the wrong method for this regime.

This thesis makes two original contributions. The first is a mechanistically attributed negative result on a published, theory-backed hypothesis. Post-hoc kNN localisation of the context [@nagler2023statistical_foundations_pfn; @thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning] does not transfer to fraud-grade imbalance, a regime in which it had not been validated. The result confirms two adverse priors from the literature, that random selection is a strong baseline [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn] and that naive distance retrieval can degrade under imbalance [@pham2026aware]. The second contribution is the positive counterpart. A cheap, tuning-free stratified context puts zero-shot TFMs above methodologically sound external state of the art on banksim and at par on eu_cc and fifar, as reported in @sec-results-sota, and the ranking-metric invariance argument of @sec-bg-eval shows the gain is genuine discrimination, not calibration. Reporting recall at fixed false-positive rates on these datasets, which the surveyed literature largely omits, is a side contribution.

The negative result is bounded by the evaluated design space: frozen TFMs, kNN retrieval with cosine distance, fraud prevalences below 1.5 % and ranking metrics. Four of the five datasets are simulations, and heterogeneous production-scale transaction streams are where relevance would have its best chance, as discussed in @sec-limitations. Within these bounds the conclusion is unambiguous. Context construction is a real test-time lever for in-context tabular learners, and this thesis shows which end of it moves: the class ratio, not relevance. Whether that holds on real, heterogeneous transaction data is the open question.
